On the Origin of the Sacred Carthusian Order

b.bio: Zacharias Ferreri (recorded in Vatican catalogues under the name 'Zacharias, Benedictus'), born in Vicenza to a noble family, entered Monte Cassino as a Benedictine but left at twenty-five for Rome, taking degrees in law and theology. He served Julius II, joined the Pisan conciliabulum of 1511 and was excommunicated in 1513, then reconciled with Leo X, who set him to prepare a shortened breviary. He was titular bishop of Sebaste (1518) and bishop of Guardialfiera (in office 1519 and 1521–1524), and in 1520–21 papal legate to Poland and Lithuania, mediating the Polish–Teutonic truce. A VIAF record links this name to an elegy on the death of Antonio Suriano, the Venetian patriarch. Zacharias Rhetor (c. 465–after 536), bishop of Mytilene, is a different author entirely.
b.s: A minor Italian humanist churchman remembered chiefly as a Latin poet and liturgical reformer; the library holds under his name a history of the Carthusian order whose polemic against the schools of Paris and themes of exile, death, and hidden reprobation mark it as monastic rather than scholastic writing.

b.bio: The library holds one three-page sermon on Saint George under this name, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 186. The sermon allegorizes persecution and baptism: God bounds the raging sea of persecutors as he bounded the sea at creation, faith founded on Christ the rock withstands trial, and the baptized must put off the old man and clothe themselves in virtues acquired by laborious discipline. No source consulted identifies this preacher's see or dates. the surviving records describe Zacharias of Mytilene (Zacharias Rhetor/Scholasticus), a late-fifth-century Miaphysite lawyer turned bishop and ecclesiastical historian born near Gaza; his known works are a church history and lives of Peter the Iberian and Severus of Antioch, not Latin sermons on Saint George. He is therefore treated as a namesake, not this author, and no biographical detail from those sources is used here.
b.s: The single held work is a brief martyrdom sermon that reads persecution through creation imagery and baptismal theology, exhorting believers to imitate Saint George.
